title: Amṛtasiddhi

attribution.tradition: ascribed in its colophon/Tibetan transmission to Virūpākṣa (identified with the Buddhist mahāsiddha Virūpa)
attribution.scholarly: anonymous Buddhist tantric (Vajrayāna) milieu with Śaiva elements; authorship uncertain

scholarly.text: c. 11th c. CE; a manuscript dated 1160 CE gives a terminus ante quem

structure.description: 36 short chapters (viveka) — c. 300 verses (as recalled; check the Mallinson–Szántó edition)

summary: The earliest known text to teach the methods later called haṭha: bindu, identified with the moon in the head, is the essence of life and is consumed by the sun (fire) in the belly; by mahāmudrā, mahābandha and mahāvedha the breath is forced into the central channel, bindu is made steady and the yogin attains the 'nectar of immortality'. It also first teaches the four stages (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti). Its setting is Buddhist tantric, with Śaiva elements.

editions.name: J. Mallinson & P.-D. Szántó, The Amṛtasiddhi and Amṛtasiddhimūla: the earliest texts of the haṭhayoga tradition (Pondicherry: IFP/EFEO 2021)

notes: Chapter count and attribution recalled, not checked: low confidence on details. U49 documents the Buddhist→haṭha borrowing.

title: Dattātreyayogaśāstra

attribution.tradition: taught by Dattātreya to the sage Sāṅkṛti in the Naimiṣa forest
attribution.scholarly: anonymous, probably composed in a Vaiṣṇava milieu, c. 13th c.

structure.description: vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments/Kokaje); Mallinson's critical text c. 334 verses

summary: The first text to teach a system it calls haṭhayoga. Dattātreya names four yogas — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja (the best) — and four stages; he teaches the eight-limbed yoga 'known to Yājñavalkya and others' and the haṭha of 'Kapila and the others' (mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, the three bandhas, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī with amarolī and sahajolī). Success comes from practice to anyone — brāhmaṇa, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist.

editions.name: vulgate e-text (sanskritdocuments.org; eBhāratī Sampat, ed. R. Kokaje)
J. Mallinson, critical edition and translation (in progress/2020s)

title: Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā (Yogakāṇḍa)

attribution.tradition: taught by the sage Vasiṣṭha to his son Śakti
attribution.scholarly: anonymous; an orthodox (Vedic-smārta) yoga text on which the Yoga Yājñavalkya draws

structure.description: the yoga section (yogakāṇḍa) in several chapters; exact count not recalled

summary: An eight-limbed yoga for the twice-born framed by Vedic orthodoxy: yamas and niyamas, a few postures, the channels and kuṇḍalinī, breath-control, a withdrawal (pratyāhāra) that moves the breath through the eighteen vital points (marma), concentration on the elements, meditation and samādhi. It is among the early texts that teach kuṇḍalinī outside a tantric frame and is named as an authority on postures in HYP 1.18.

editions.name: Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā (Yoga Kāṇḍa), Kaivalyadhama, Lonavla (1969; rev. 2005)

notes: Distinct from the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (src:yoga-vasistha). Chapter structure not recalled: low confidence.

title: Vivekamārtaṇḍa

attribution.scholarly: early Nāth-affiliated text, c. 13th c.; the source of the widely printed 'Gorakṣaśataka' (src:goraksasataka) and Gorakṣapaddhati recensions

summary: A six-limbed yoga (āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi) that joins Kaula body-mapping to haṭha method: siddhāsana and padmāsana, the centres, the channels and breaths, kuṇḍalinī, the seals and locks (mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā/khecarī, uḍḍiyāna, jālandhara, mūlabandha), viparītakaraṇī for the nectar, the five element concentrations, meditation with and without qualities and samādhi.
notes: Close verbal parallels with src:goraksasataka (U21 owns that entry; refs there follow the Kuvalayananda–Shukla numbering). U21 flags src:yogamartanda as possibly another member of this family.

title: Yogabīja

attribution.tradition: a dialogue of Īśvara (Śiva) and Devī, ascribed to Gorakṣa

summary: Argues that knowledge alone does not liberate: the body must be 'ripened' (pakva) in the fire of yoga, for an unripe body is subject to karma and rebirth. It teaches the great yoga (mahāyoga) that unites mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja, and gives what is probably the earliest statement that 'ha' is the sun and 'ṭha' the moon, their union being haṭha.

editions.name: Yogabīja, ed. Rāmlāl Śrīvāstav (Gorakhpur: Gorakhnath Mandir 1982)

notes: The ha/ṭha verse is quoted in Brahmānanda's Jyotsnā (on HYP 1.1) as from the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati; scholars (J. Birch) locate it in the Yogabīja — recalled, check.

title: Śārṅgadhara Paddhati (yoga section)

attribution.scholarly: anthology completed 1363 CE; its yoga section draws on earlier haṭha and rājayoga texts

structure.description: a large anthology (c. 4,700 verses) with a yoga section near the end

summary: A 14th-c. verse anthology whose yoga section is among the earliest datable witnesses to haṭha: it distinguishes two kinds of haṭha — one practised by Gorakṣa and others, another by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu (Mārkaṇḍeya) and others — and quotes rājayoga and haṭha verses shared with the Dattātreyayogaśāstra and Amaraughaprabodha.
notes: The two kinds of haṭha are recalled with moderate-low confidence (check). Not the Āyurvedic Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā (src:sarngadhara-samhita).

title: Khecarīvidyā

attribution.tradition: taught by Ādinātha (Śiva) to the Goddess

scholarly.text: c. 14th c. CE (before the Haṭhapradīpikā, which borrows from it)

summary: The fullest text on khecarī mudrā: a secret mantra that must be received from a guru, a physical practice on the tongue so that it can enter the cavity above the palate, the drinking of the nectar of immortality from the moon in the head, the places and kalās of the nectar, and (in its last chapter) herbal preparations. RESTRICTED: recorded here as summary with the text's own warnings only; no procedure is given.

editions.name: J. Mallinson, The Khecarīvidyā of Ādinātha (London: Routledge 2007), critical edition and translation

title: Yoga Yājñavalkya

attribution.scholarly: anonymous orthodox text dependent on the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā, c. 13th–14th c.

summary: An eight-limbed yoga for Vedic householders and renouncers taught by Yājñavalkya to Gārgī: ten yamas and ten niyamas, postures, the channels and the ten breaths, purification of the channels, breath-control with Vedic mantra, a fivefold withdrawal including the movement of breath through the eighteen vital points, the five element concentrations, meditation and samādhi. It allows women and śūdras to practise with non-Vedic mantras (recalled).

editions.name: Yogayājñavalkya, ed. P. C. Divanji (Bombay: BBRAS 1954)

notes: Not the Yājñavalkya Smṛti nor the Bṛhadyogiyājñavalkya Smṛti. The provision for women and śūdras is recalled with low confidence.

title: Yogatārāvalī

attribution.scholarly: not by the author of the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya; c. 14th c., before the Haṭhapradīpikā

summary: A short poem on rājayoga reached through absorption in the inner sound: nādānusandhāna is the foremost of the layas, the three bandhas and spontaneous (kevala) retention lead to the mindless state (amanaska) and the natural state (sahaja), in which the yogin is freed from the world while living.

title: Amanaska (Amanaskayoga)

attribution.tradition: a dialogue of Īśvara and Vāmadeva; sometimes ascribed to Gorakṣa
attribution.scholarly: two originally separate chapters: ch. 2 c. 11th–12th c., ch. 1 later

scholarly.text: ch. 2 c. 11th–12th c.; ch. 1 by c. 1400

summary: The principal text of a rājayoga called 'mindlessness' (amanaska): by a gaze without object and the guru's grace the mind dissolves effortlessly, the breath stops of itself and the yogin attains liberation while living. Its second chapter dismisses laborious methods — breath-control, mudrās, mantra-repetition, meditation on objects, pilgrimage, scriptural study — as useless or harmful beside this natural state.

editions.name: J. Birch, The Amanaska: King of All Yogas (D.Phil. Oxford 2013), critical edition and translation

title: Śiva Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: the words of Śiva (Īśvara) to Pārvatī
attribution.scholarly: anonymous, probably from the region of Vārāṇasī, c. 15th c.; draws on Śrīvidyā and Advaita

structure.description: 5 paṭalas (c. 510–645 verses depending on edition; the Muktabodha e-text has c. 514)

summary: A yoga manual addressed also to householders. Ch. 1 surveys and rejects rival doctrines and teaches a non-dual Vedānta; ch. 2 maps the body as a microcosm (Meru, moon and sun, 350,000 channels, fourteen principal); ch. 3 the breaths, the guru, the conditions and four stages of practice and the postures; ch. 4 the mudrās; ch. 5 the obstacles, the four yogas and four grades of aspirant, the centres, rājayoga at the thousand-petalled lotus (Kailāsa) and a Śrīvidyā mantra practice.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing)
J. Mallinson, The Shiva Samhita (Woodstock NY: YogaVidya.com 2007)

title: Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā (Haṭhapradīpikā)

attribution.tradition: by Svātmārāma, who received haṭhavidyā through the grace of Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the Siddhas (1.4)
attribution.scholarly: compiled by Svātmārāma c. mid-15th c. from some twenty earlier texts (Amṛtasiddhi, DYŚ, Vivekamārtaṇḍa, Khecarīvidyā, Amaraughaprabodha, Amanaska and others)

tradition.text: in the succession of Ādinātha, Matsyendra and Gorakṣa

structure.description: vulgate: 4 upadeśas, c. 389 verses (āsana; prāṇāyāma and ṣaṭkarma; mudrā; samādhi/nādānusandhāna). A longer recension in 10 chapters is also transmitted.

summary: The classic compendium of haṭha, taught 'solely for rājayoga'. Upadeśa 1: lineage, secrecy, the hut, what destroys and promotes yoga, postures, diet. 2: breath-control, the purification of the channels, the six cleansing acts and the eight retentions, with warnings about improper practice. 3: kuṇḍalinī and the ten mudrās (including khecarī and vajrolī). 4: samādhi and its synonyms, the dissolution of mind and breath, śāmbhavī, the four stages and the inner sounds (nādānusandhāna), and the liberated yogin.

editions.name: The Haṭhayogapradīpikā with the Jyotsnā of Brahmānanda (Adyar Library 1893; 1972)
Haṭhapradīpikā, critical edition, Kaivalyadhama (Lonavla 1970; 10-chapter recension 1998)
GRETIL and sanskrit/raw_etexts e-texts

title: Jyotsnā (commentary on the Haṭhapradīpikā)

structure.description: running commentary on all four upadeśas

summary: The standard Sanskrit commentary: it glosses haṭha as the union of 'ha' (sun, prāṇa) and 'ṭha' (moon, apāna), i.e. prāṇāyāma, and rājayoga as asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity; it discusses who is eligible (the dispassionate, per the Vāyu Saṃhitā, Sureśvara and Yājñavalkya), explains the practices, and reads the text through Pātañjala yoga and Advaita.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00243; Adyar Library edition

title: Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: the teaching of the sage Gheraṇḍa to Caṇḍakāpāli

structure.description: 7 upadeśas, c. 350 verses (Thomi ed.: 62 + 46 + 102 + 19 + 99 + 24 + 24 lines of numbering)

summary: Teaches 'yoga of the pot' (ghaṭastha-yoga): the body, an unbaked pot, is fired in yoga through seven means — the cleansing acts (purification), postures (firmness), mudrās (steadiness), withdrawal (calm), breath-control (lightness), meditation (direct perception of the self) and samādhi (non-attachment, liberation). It lists 32 postures, 25 mudrās, many variants of the six acts, eight retentions, three kinds of meditation and six kinds of samādhi.

editions.name: Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā, ed. P. Thomi (Wichtrach 1993); GRETIL e-text
J. Mallinson, The Gheranda Samhita (YogaVidya.com 2004)

title: Haṭharatnāvalī
summary: A haṭha manual that often argues with the Haṭhapradīpikā: it teaches eight cleansing acts (aṣṭakarma, adding cakrī and gajakaraṇī), the retentions and ten mudrās, names eighty-four postures and describes a selection, and treats the channels, centres, the inner sound and samādhi. It holds that mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja are one 'great yoga'.

editions.name: Haṭharatnāvalī of Śrīnivāsayogī, ed. M. L. Gharote, P. Devnath, V. K. Jha (Lonavla 2002)

notes: Contents recalled in outline; the Andhra provenance is a low-confidence recollection.

title: Jogapradīpikā (Jogapradīpyakā)

attribution.scholarly: composed 1737 CE in Braj Bhāṣā; the author belonged to a Vaiṣṇava (Rāmānandī) milieu (recalled)

summary: A vernacular compendium of haṭha that teaches eighty-four postures and twenty-four mudrās, the cleansing acts, retentions, the centres and meditation; the illustrated manuscripts of this text are among the main visual sources for pre-modern postures.
notes: Dating and counts recalled; the Rāmānandī affiliation is low-confidence.

title: Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati

structure.description: prose sections on yamas and niyamas, cleansing, c. 112 postures, breath, mudrās and nāda

summary: A prose manual notable for describing more than a hundred postures, including many dynamic and rope postures not found in earlier texts, set within a sequence of yama, niyama, ṣaṭkarma, āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā and nāda.
notes: Known mainly through J. Birch's studies (recalled). Author name, count of postures and provenance low confidence.

title: Śiva Svarodaya

scholarly.text: uncertain; probably mid–late second millennium CE

summary: The science of the flow of breath (svara) in the left (iḍā, moon), right (piṅgalā, sun) and central (suṣumnā) channels: the daily alternation of the nostrils, the five elements (tattvas) that arise in each flow, which actions suit which flow, and the use of the breath to foretell events and death. The central flow suits only meditation.
notes: Verse numbers not recalled; teachings cite sections.

title: Śrītattvacintāmaṇi

structure.description: a Śākta digest in many chapters (prakāśa); ch. 6 is the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa

summary: Pūrṇānanda's digest of Śākta tantric practice, whose sixth chapter circulates separately as the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa.

title: Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa
summary: A detailed description of the six centres along the central channel (citriṇī within vajrā within suṣumnā) and the thousand-petalled lotus above: for each, its petals and letters, element and seed-syllable, deity and śakti; then the rousing of kuṇḍalinī, her ascent through the centres dissolving each element into the next, her union with Paramaśiva and her return. Made known in the West by Arthur Avalon's The Serpent Power (1919).

editions.name: Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe), The Serpent Power (London 1919), with Kālīcaraṇa's commentary

title: Pādukāpañcaka

scholarly.text: uncertain; before the 18th-c. commentary of Kālīcaraṇa

summary: 'The Five-fold Footstool': a hymn on the guru's sandals (pādukā) meditated upon in the thousand-petalled lotus — the white lotus, the triangle of the letters a-ka-tha, the haṃsa, the two sandals of light and the jewelled seat — as the culmination of the inner ascent.

editions.name: in Avalon, The Serpent Power (1919)

title: Haṭhatattvakaumudī

attribution.tradition: by Sundaradeva of Kāśī, son of Govindadeva, grandson of Viśvanāthadeva, of the Kāśyapa gotra (colophon)

structure.description: 56 chapters (udyota) grouped in ullāsas, the last (9th) on rājayoga (Lonavla edition)

summary: A large compendium of haṭha that quotes and systematizes earlier texts: yamas and niyamas, the eight cleansing acts, postures, many retentions (including raising and lowering kinds), the three bandhas and mudrās, vajrolī, kuṇḍalinī and śakticālana, the channels and breaths, the sixteen supports, the centres, nāda, saguṇa and nirguṇa meditation, saṃyama and its powers, rājayoga, the signs of approaching death and the cheating of death.

editions.name: Haṭhatattvakaumudī of Sundaradeva, ed. M. L. Gharote, P. Devnath, V. K. Jha (Lonavla 2007)

notes: Chapter titles checked against the local eBhāratī e-text (colophons).

title: Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā
summary: Sundaradeva's second haṭha compendium, known from manuscripts; it collects postures, breath and mudrā teachings from earlier texts.
notes: Existence recalled from J. Birch's work on Sundaradeva; contents not recalled.

title: Yuktabhavadeva

structure.description: chapters on the eight limbs with haṭha material (not recalled in detail)

summary: A 17th-c. compendium that integrates haṭha practices — postures, cleansing, retentions, mudrās — into the eight-limbed framework of Pātañjala yoga.

editions.name: Yuktabhavadeva of Bhavadeva Miśra, ed. M. L. Gharote & V. K. Jha (Lonavla 2002)

title: Yogacintāmaṇi (of Śivānanda Sarasvatī)

attribution.tradition: by Śivānanda Sarasvatī, pupil of Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī (colophons)

summary: A compilation of citations on yoga from many works (Purāṇas, Yoga Sūtra, haṭha texts) with the author's commentary, arranged by the limbs of yoga, and quoted by later commentators (Brahmānanda cites 'the author of the Yogacintāmaṇi' on eligibility).

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00536 (from NGMCP B 39/5)

notes: Distinct from a Yogacintāmaṇi ascribed to Godāvaramiśra. Structure and colophons checked in the local e-text.

title: Kumbhakapaddhati
summary: A manual devoted to breath-retention (kumbhaka), describing many more kinds than the HYP's eight. RESTRICTED as to method: only its existence and scope are recorded.

editions.name: Kumbhaka Paddhati of Raghuvīra, ed. M. L. Gharote (Lonavla 2000)

title: Ṣaṭkarmasaṅgraha
summary: A manual on the cleansing acts (ṣaṭkarma) and their many variants, together with the diseases they are said to cure.
notes: Author and date are low-confidence recollections (Lonavla edition by Gharote, 1990s).

title: Śrītattvanidhi

attribution.tradition: compiled under Mummaḍi Kṛṣṇarāja Woḍeyar III of Mysore

structure.description: an encyclopaedia of iconography in nine 'treasures' (nidhi); a section illustrates c. 122 postures

summary: A Mysore court encyclopaedia of deities and sacred lore whose illustrated section on postures (drawing on the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati) preserves over a hundred āsanas, many of them dynamic.
notes: Posture count and dependence on the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati recalled (N. E. Sjoman; J. Birch).
